text.p: Serbia's political opposition and President Slobodan Milosevic remained deadlocked as marathon street protests against local election fraud showed no signs of abating.
"It is really a deadly game of 'chicken' they are playing but whatever the outcome Milosevic has already lost a lot," a senior western diplomat said.
Serbia's opposition alliance believes time is running out for the autocratic Milosevic, amid signs that state authority is weakening in the face of protests in their 77th day on Saturday.

"They say Milosevic's tactic is to keep buying time -- but every day we persevere is a defeat for him and a victory for us -- time is on our side," Zoran Djindjic told tens of thousands of cheering supporters of the opposition Zajedno coalition.
Each side has shown signs of cracking during the last two and a half months.

Protest rallies have sometimes waned, encouraging Milosevic's camp to endure just a little bit longer. Then, at crucial moments, more demonstrators have turned out to give fresh impetus to Zajedno leaders.

In Rome, the international community's High Representative for Bosnia, Carl Bildt said on Friday Serbia was becoming the "sick man of Europe" with no way out of desperate economic straits unless Milosevic honoured the opposition's election wins.

Economic experts say the new Yugoslav federation has lost hundreds of millions of desperately needed dollars for recosntruction of its sanctions-hit economy after potential investors baulked at the crisis.

The latest and perhaps the worst in the terms of confidence ratings abroad came from the British banking group National Westminster Plc on Friday, whose cooperation last year with Belgrade was much publicized in the domestic press.
The financial institution said it had withdrawn from its role as adviser to the federal Yugoslav government on negotiations with the Balkan nation's international creditors.
A spokeswoman said the decision followed recent signs that Belgrade had moved away from commitments to economic liberalisation and democratisation.

"We have indicated to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that, due to the change in the international climate, we are unable to proceed with our advisory work with them on sovereign debt negotiations," the spokeswoman said.

She said Belgrade gave commitments to greater economic and political liberalism at the time of the Dayton negotiations which brought peace to Bosnia, but added that "recent actions by the Republic have shown a move away from that commitment".
Yugoslavia is waiting to begin talks with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank on repaying a total of $1.3 billion to the two institutions.
It needs to agree terms on this debt before it can expect new loans to help it rebuild an economy shattered by the Bosnian conflict.
"This is a bitter blow to Milosevic who was counting on the Dayton accord to pay off in terms of foreign assistance and kick-start development necessary for his relection," the diplomat said.
With fresh foreign capital out of bounds, Milosevic is facing increasing dissent from his party, police and the army and threats of more strikes as lawyers and teachers stopped work.
